title: Calendar embeds and the trust around them
metaTitle: Booking pages that explain the meeting
excerpt: Repeat what the meeting is for and how long it lasts before the calendar appears. A naked booking widget feels like a trap, not an invitation.
alt: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen. The calm corridor fits a piece about a booking page that should feel clear before anyone picks a time.
caption: The meeting should be explained before the time is chosen. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a booking page say besides the calendar?
faqs.answer: What the meeting is for, how long it is, and what the other person should bring or need not prepare. The time zone should be visible before they confirm. A page that is only a grid of slots asks them to commit before they understand the conversation.

faqs.question: Are embedded calendars bad?
faqs.answer: No. An embed is a reasonable way to show real availability, and the trust problem is a naked embed with no sentence around it and no hint of who they will meet. Put your header, your explanation, and your length above or beside the widget. After they book, confirm the time in your own words as well as in the tool's email.

faqs.question: How long should the meeting be?
faqs.answer: As long as the decision you are trying to make, and no longer. Say the number on the page. A short intro that exists to see if there is a fit should not be described as a workshop. If you need two lengths, label them by outcome, not by a vague 'quick chat' and 'deep dive.'

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The booking page should repeat what the meeting is for and how long it is, in your words, before anyone stares at a grid of times. That is booking page design. A naked calendar feels like a trap. The slots are real. The intention is hidden. People hesitate, or they book and arrive defensive.

Nielsen Norman Group's visit research is a fair clock here. People often decide in the first 10 to 20 seconds whether a page is worth staying with, and the value has to be clear inside about 10 seconds if you want more of their attention. On this page the value is a specific conversation. Name it at the top. Then show the times.

## Say the purpose and the length

Write the purpose as an outcome. "See whether a studio engagement is a fit, and what a first project would need." That tells a founder what they are walking into. "Intro call" alone is a label. Pair it with the length in the same breath. Thirty minutes is a different promise from an hour, and both are different from an open-ended demo.

Say who is in the meeting if it is always the same shape. A founder talking with the person who will do the work is a different meeting from a founder talking with a coordinator who will only route them. You do not need a biography. You need the role. If the person varies, say that a member of the team will host, and keep that true.

Say what it is not. Not a hard sell with a deck they cannot leave. Not a requirement to have a brief finished. Not a support channel for an existing product, if that belongs elsewhere. Boundaries make the yes easier. People decline calendars when they fear a long, shapeless hour.

Put this text in HTML you control, not only inside the embed's title field. Embed titles are easy to leave on a default, and they are easy to lose when the tool restyles itself. Your page is the frame. The tool is the availability.

## What a naked embed feels like

A full-width calendar with no header is a widget from another company. The type does not match. The button does not match. The stranger's first question is whether they are still on your site. That question is a tax on trust before they have picked a slot.

Some tools invite you to "just share your link." A raw link can be right in an email to someone who already knows you. It is wrong as the only public path from a homepage, where the visitor may be one sentence into understanding what you do. The page around the link is the context the email would have carried.

Watch the height. A tall embed that pushes your explanation below the fold on a phone has recreated the naked calendar. The purpose should be visible without scrolling. The first times can sit just under it. If the embed is an iframe that grows without warning and shoves your paragraph away, fix the frame. A page that jumps when the widget finishes loading feels unreliable at the exact moment you are asking for a commitment.

Read the embed's own copy. Defaults like "Book a meeting" or "Powered by" are fine when they are quiet. Defaults that contradict your length, your cancellation rule, or your price are not fine. Turn off the extra questions the tool added on its own. Every extra field is a reason to abandon a decision they had already almost made.

## Time zones, buffers, and honesty

Show the zone, and show it before the confirm button. A founder in another country should not discover the offset in the email afterward. Good tools detect a zone and label it. Your job is to make sure the label is visible and that the confirmation repeats it. "10:00" without a zone is how two people miss each other and both feel stood up.

Buffers and notice periods should match the sentence on the page. If you cannot meet tomorrow, do not let the calendar offer tomorrow. If you need ten minutes between calls, set that in the tool rather than apologizing when you are late. The grid is a claim about your week. Make the claim true.

Cancellation and reschedule belong in one line near the button. "You can move the time from the email we send." That line removes the fear of a wrong click. Hide the policy in a footer and people will either bail or book a slot they already know is bad. Do not charge a fee you have not explained, and do not threaten one in the tool's small print if you would never collect it.

If the meeting is paid, the price and what it includes have to be on this page, not only on a checkout step that appears after they have invested in a time. A surprise invoice is the trap version of a calendar. Free or paid, the terms are part of the invitation.

## The page around the widget

Use your header, your type, and your primary button styles where you control them. The embed will look a bit foreign. The frame should not. A founder should feel they are still in the same site they were just reading, because they are.

Offer a way to write instead, for the person who cannot find a slot or who is not ready to pick one. A single mail link, with a sentence about what to include, is enough. Do not make it louder than the calendar if booking is the path you want. Do make it real. A calendar with no escape forces a fit that is not there, and those meetings go poorly.

Repeat a piece of proof only if it helps the decision to book. One line about the kind of work, or a link to a relevant project, can steady a nervous buyer. A carousel of testimonials beside the grid distracts from the time. They are in the decision. Help them finish it.

On a phone, check that you can pick a time without zooming, that the confirm button stays reachable, and that the page does not scroll them back to the top when the widget redraws. Test a real booking with a colleague in another zone if you have one. Read the email that arrives. It should sound like you.

## After they book

The screen that follows is a confirmation. It needs the purpose, the length, the time, the zone, and how to change it. The tool will send an email. You should still look at that email and align the words. If you send a second note from a person, it should add something the tool cannot: where to look in the meantime, or what you will ask first. It should not arrive as a wall of preparation they did not agree to.

Send a reminder that respects the length. A reminder an hour before is useful. A sequence of five emails is how a short intro starts to feel like a campaign. Put the link to join in the reminder, and make the link the same one that was in the invite. New links at the last minute look like phishing even when they are not.

If they do not show, have a human response that assumes a mistake. A short note with a way to rebook beats a scolding automation. You learn more from a reply than from a no-show tag. The calendar is a tool for a conversation. The conversation includes the misses.

Keep the public page up to date when your availability or your offer changes. A booking page for a service you no longer take is worse than no page. Unpublish the path, or change the sentence and the calendar together. Do it in the same week. Stale slots are how you end up in meetings you resent, with people who were told the wrong story.

## A ten-minute review

Open the page in a private window, as if you were a stranger. In one breath, say what the meeting is, how long it is, and what it will not be. If you have to click into the widget to learn any of those, move the words up. Then book a real slot, reschedule it, and cancel it. Each email should be recognizable and accurate.

Ask one person outside the company to do the same and tell you where they hesitated. Hesitation on the grid is often a missing fact, not a shortage of open times. Add the fact. Do not add more branding to the iframe.

The page is done when a skeptical founder can choose a time without feeling handled. That is a writing task and a settings task. The embed is the easy part.

If you want to see how a short intro is framed before you build your own, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Notice what you needed to know before you were willing to pick a time. Those are the lines your page is missing.

The words around the widget only work if a skimmer can catch them. [Writing for buyers who skim](/blog/writing-for-buyers-who-skim) is the next piece, on putting the point in the first lines and in the headings so a fast reader can still repeat the offer.
